transcript:
# Day 19, Economics and Systems Thinking: Thinking at the margin (the marginal revolution, 1871 to 1874)

Picture a cardholder who is 90 days late on a balance. Your collections team can make one more phone call tonight. Should they? The instinct is to ask whether collections calls are worth it in general. That is the wrong question. The only question that matters is this one: what does this one extra call cost, and what will this one extra call bring in? Not the average call. The next one.

That is thinking at the margin. The margin is the edge of a decision, the next unit of something: the next hour of work, the next dollar spent, the next hire, the next slice of pizza. Marginal cost is what that next unit costs you. Marginal benefit is what it gets you. The rule is almost embarrassingly simple: keep going as long as the marginal benefit beats the marginal cost, and stop when they meet. Economists call that meeting point the optimum.

Why does this matter? Because most of us decide using totals and averages, and totals and averages hide the decision. A team that has already run 2,000 collections calls this month has an average return per call. But the first 500 calls went to people who were about to pay anyway. Call number 2,001 goes to someone who has ignored twenty messages. The average looks great. The margin is probably negative. If you manage by the average, you keep spending. If you manage by the margin, you stop.

The idea has a history. For most of the 1800s, economists were stuck on a puzzle Adam Smith had noticed: water is essential and cheap, diamonds are useless and expensive. Why? In the early 1870s three men working separately, William Stanley Jevons in England, Carl Menger in Austria and Leon Walras in Switzerland, gave the same answer. Value does not come from how useful a thing is in total. It comes from how useful the next unit is to you. You have plenty of water, so one more glass is worth almost nothing. You have no diamonds, so one is worth a lot. The next unit's value, not the total, sets the price. This shift is called the marginal revolution, and it is the foundation of modern microeconomics.

The strongest objection comes from how people actually behave. Herbert Simon, who you will meet later in the game theory track, argued that nobody really computes marginal costs and benefits. We do not have the information or the time. We use rules of thumb and stop at "good enough." Behavioral economists have piled on evidence that people are swayed by sunk costs, by framing, by what everyone else is doing. The marginal rule describes a calculating machine, not a person.

Defenders answer in two ways. First, the rule is a tool for deciding better, not a description of how people already decide. You do not have to be a marginal thinker by nature to become one on purpose. Second, even when individuals are sloppy, competition pushes firms and markets toward the margin over time, because the ones that ignore it lose money to the ones that respect it. Both answers have some truth. Where the idea gets overhyped is when people treat every real decision as smooth and divisible. Many are lumpy. You cannot hire half a person or build 40 percent of a bridge, and the margin gets blurry there.

This builds directly on Day 4. Opportunity cost told you that every choice has a cost: the best thing you gave up. Marginal thinking tells you where to look for that cost: at the next unit, not the whole pile. It also quietly underlies the incentives reading from Day 9. The cobra bounty in Delhi failed because people responded at the margin. One more cobra earned one more payment, so they bred one more cobra. In the psychology track, sunk cost thinking is exactly the failure to think at the margin: counting what you have already spent, which cannot be changed, instead of what the next step costs.

A question for today: pick one thing you or your team are doing more of than you should. Is the case for it built on the average return, or on the return of the next unit?

If you want the primary source, try Carl Menger's Principles of Economics (1871), chapter 3, "The Theory of Value," which works through the water and diamonds puzzle in plain prose and is far easier reading than Jevons.
